prompt: When does a Spring Boot application, built the way this course builds the bookshop, work out which beans exist and which one each constructor receives?

choices.text: Every time it starts
choices.why: Right. The container scans the package, reads constructors by reflection and checks the autoconfiguration conditions on each start, and keeps none of it for the next one.

choices.text: While `javac` compiles the classes
choices.why: That is Micronaut's moment. Spring's compiler step produces ordinary classes and nothing about the wiring.

choices.text: During `mvn package`, when the jar is built
choices.why: That is where Quarkus does it, and where Spring's optional AOT step would. The bookshop does not use that step.

choices.text: The first time a request reaches each controller
choices.why: Spring builds its singleton beans before it opens the port, which is why a missing bean stops the start instead of failing a request.

prompt: In which of these deployments do a few seconds of startup cost the most?
hint: Count how often a user waits for a start.

choices.text: A monolith deployed once a week and kept running
choices.why: It pays the start once a week. Nobody waits on it except the person deploying.

choices.text: A service with heavy traffic that runs on three long-lived instances
choices.why: Heavy traffic is a question of throughput once running. The three starts happen at deploy time and the users never see them.

choices.text: A nightly batch job that runs for two hours
choices.why: A few seconds out of two hours is noise, and nobody is waiting for the first answer.

choices.text: A function that is started from zero copies when a request arrives
choices.why: Right. Every cold start is a user waiting, so the startup time is part of the response time.

prompt: A Quarkus service is deployed, and the operator changes a property in its environment and restarts it. The new value is ignored. What is the likeliest explanation?
hint: Not every property is read at the same moment.

choices.text: It is a build-time property, so it needs a new build
choices.why: Right. Work moved into the build is decided there, and Quarkus marks such properties as build-time ones; changing them at start does nothing.

choices.text: Quarkus never reads the environment, only the properties file
choices.why: Properties read at start can come from the environment, as in Spring. The issue is which properties are read at start at all.

choices.text: A native image cannot read configuration at all
choices.why: A native image still reads runtime configuration when it starts; what it cannot do is change what was decided in its build.

choices.text: The restart reused a cached container from the last start
choices.why: Quarkus keeps no container between starts; what it replays is a record made by the build, which is the point.

prompt: Which of these does Spring Boot do at every start that Micronaut has already done while compiling? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of the container's work, not the server's.

choices.text: Scanning the package for annotated classes
choices.why: Right. Micronaut's annotation processors saw every annotation inside `javac`.

choices.text: Reading constructors by reflection to find what each bean needs
choices.why: Right. Micronaut generated a class per bean that calls the constructor directly.

choices.text: Opening the HTTP port
choices.why: Every server opens its port when it starts; a port cannot be opened by a compiler.

choices.text: Reading the values of runtime properties such as the database password
choices.why: Both read runtime configuration at start, since a password must not be compiled into the program.

prompt: Match each framework to where it works out its wiring.
hint: The figure in the first reading section.
right_distractors: an operator, when the service is deployed

prompt: In a Play application, a route in `conf/routes` names a controller method that was renamed. When does the mistake show?
hint: The routes file is not read at start.

choices.text: At start, when Guice builds the controllers and their routes
choices.why: Guice runs at start, but the routes file was turned into code long before that.

choices.text: In the build, because the routes file is compiled into code
choices.why: Right. A route naming a method that does not exist is a compile error, and nothing is deployed with it.

choices.text: Only when a request reaches that route
choices.why: That would be the behaviour of routes read by reflection at request time; Play's are checked earlier.

choices.text: Never: the route silently answers 404
choices.why: A route that silently disappeared would be the worst outcome, and compiling the file is how Play avoids it.

prompt: Why is producing a GraalVM native image simpler for Quarkus and Micronaut than for a Spring Boot application left as this course builds it?
hint: What has to be declared before a native image is built?

choices.text: GraalVM only accepts Jakarta annotations, which Spring does not use
choices.why: native-image compiles any Java; it knows nothing about which annotations a framework chose.

choices.text: Spring's jar is too large for native-image to compile
choices.why: Size makes the build slower, not impossible. The obstacle is reflection, not bytes.

choices.text: Everything reached by reflection must be known before the build, and their wiring is already decided then
choices.why: Right. A framework that wires at start by reflection has to run that analysis early first, which is the job of Spring's AOT step.

choices.text: A native image cannot open a network port without Jetty
choices.why: A native image opens sockets like any program; Spring's Tomcat works in one too once the AOT step has run.

prompt: Micronaut wires the application at compile time: its annotation processors run inside ___ and write a class for every bean.
A Micronaut Data repository declares `findByTitel` where the entity's field is `title`. When does the team find out?
hint: Micronaut Data builds the query from the method name, and the question is when.

choices.text: When the application starts and builds the repository
choices.why: That is when Spring Data would complain about a derived query; Micronaut Data has already parsed the name by then.

choices.text: The first time the method is called
choices.why: Nothing about this query is left to the call; the name was checked earlier.

choices.text: Never: the method returns an empty list
choices.why: A query naming a field that does not exist is refused, not run against nothing.

choices.text: When the code is compiled
choices.why: Right. The annotation processor turns the name into a query inside javac and fails the build on a field that does not exist, so the typo never reaches a running application.

prompt: The first build of `javalin-hello` had no Jackson in its pom, and `GET /books` answered 500. What does that show about Javalin?
hint: Compare it with what lesson 4's starters did for the bookshop.

choices.text: Records cannot be turned into JSON outside Spring
choices.why: The same record became JSON as soon as jackson-databind was in the pom.

choices.text: Javalin needs an annotation on the handler to know it returns JSON
choices.why: Javalin reads no annotations; `ctx.json` is the whole instruction, and it needs a mapper to carry it out.

choices.text: You choose and add the JSON library; Spring's starter had brought one
choices.why: Right. spring-boot-starter-webmvc pulls in Jackson and configures it; a library leaves that decision, and its absence, to you.

choices.text: Port 7070 was still held by the run before, so the server answered with an error
choices.why: A taken port stops the server from starting at all; this server started and answered, with a 500.

prompt: Why does the `javalin-hello` pom carry the maven-shade-plugin?
hint: Lesson 1 tried to run a jar that needed a library.

choices.text: To make the classes smaller by renaming their packages as it copies them
choices.why: The plugin can relocate packages, but this pom does not ask it to; the jar it produces is bigger, not smaller.

choices.text: Because Javalin refuses to start from a jar that the ordinary jar plugin made
choices.why: Javalin does not know how it was packaged. The plain jar fails before Javalin is reached, because its classes are not in it.

choices.text: To pack every dependency into one runnable jar, main class named
choices.why: Right. The plain jar holds only `HelloApp`; the shaded one holds Javalin, Jetty, Jackson and the logger too.

choices.text: To pin the versions of the dependencies
choices.why: Versions are pinned by the `<version>` of each dependency; shading copies whatever was resolved.

prompt: Put in order what happens between `java -jar` and the answer to `GET /books/2` in `javalin-hello`.
hint: Configuration comes before the server; the handler before the JSON.
items: `main` calls `Javalin.create`, and the lambda registers the two routes
Jetty accepts the request and Javalin matches it to `/books/{id}`
The handler converts `{id}`, finds the book and calls `ctx.json`
Jackson writes the record as JSON in the response
trap: In Javalin 7 the routes are part of the configuration, so they are registered before the port opens, not after.

prompt: The bookshop's jar is 21,580,405 bytes and `javalin-hello`'s is 9,534,256. How many times bigger is the bookshop's? Answer to two decimal places.
hint: Divide the first by the second.

prompt: Why does `first-answer.sh` time the start from outside instead of comparing the line each framework prints about its own startup?

choices.text: The frameworks' lines are rounded too coarsely to compare
choices.why: Both report to the millisecond. The trouble is what they count, not how precisely.

choices.text: Each line starts its stopwatch at a different moment
choices.why: Right. Neither counts the JVM's own start, and they do not begin at the same point after it; the time from `java -jar` to the first answer is one span for both.

choices.text: Javalin does not print a startup time
choices.why: It does: `Javalin started in ...ms`, under its banner.

choices.text: Spring's line is printed before Tomcat opens the port
choices.why: Spring logs `Started` after the web server is up, so its number is not short of the port.

prompt: Over three runs each, the bookshop took about three times as long as `javalin-hello` to answer its first request. Which conclusion does that measurement support?
hint: What was timed, and how often does it happen?

choices.text: Javalin answers requests about three times faster once both are running
choices.why: The first answer was the one thing timed. Speed once running is a separate measurement, and lesson 20 takes one.

choices.text: Each start of the bookshop costs some seconds more than Javalin's, on that machine
choices.why: Right. It is a cost per start, measured on one machine, which matters exactly as often as the service starts.

choices.text: The fully built bookshop of lesson 23 will be three times slower to start than a Javalin service with the same features
choices.why: Neither of those two programs was measured. Database, security and metrics add start-up work to both.

choices.text: Spring Boot is unsuitable for production services
choices.why: Most production services start once per deploy and run for days; for them a few seconds at start go unnoticed.

prompt: Each symptom below is typical of one framework, because of where that framework does its wiring. Match them.
hint: Ask in which phase each mistake could first be noticed.

pairs.left: a route naming a renamed method breaks the build
a property changed in production takes effect only after a new build
a build without the annotation processors produces an application that finds no beans
a missing JSON library shows up as a 500 at the first request

prompt: A team runs a Spring Boot API with Spring Security and Spring Data on four instances that live for weeks. A start takes nine seconds, and somebody proposes rewriting it in Javalin to fix that. What is the strongest objection?
hint: When is the nine seconds paid, and what would the rewrite cost?

choices.text: Javalin will not run on more than one instance behind a load balancer
choices.why: A Javalin service is an ordinary process with a port, and runs on as many instances as anything else.

choices.text: Javalin has no way to talk to a database
choices.why: It can, through any library the team adds, such as JDBC from lesson 9. Choosing and wiring that library is the cost.

choices.text: Javalin also starts slowly once it has as many routes as this API
choices.why: Registering a lambda per route is cheap; nothing in this lesson suggests routes are where Spring's seconds go.

choices.text: Its starts are rare, and Spring's libraries would be lost
choices.why: Right. Startup matters when starts are frequent and waited on; here they are neither, and the ecosystem is what the team would give up.

prompt: A colleague reads `Javalin started in` a few hundred milliseconds and `Started BookshopApplication in` a few seconds, and says: "So Javalin is several times faster than Spring." What is wrong with that? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three separate questions: what each line counts, what startup says about requests, and where it was measured.

choices.text: The two lines start their stopwatches at different moments, so they are not one measurement
choices.why: Right. Compare the time from `java -jar` to the first answer instead, which is one span for both.

choices.text: Startup time says nothing about how fast each answers once running
choices.why: Right. "Faster" for a service usually means requests, and that is a load test, not a start.

choices.text: A single run on one machine is not a measurement of the frameworks in general
choices.why: Right. The lesson's own runs differed from each other by hundreds of milliseconds or more.

choices.text: Spring's number leaves out the time Tomcat takes to open the port
choices.why: Spring prints `Started` after the web server is up; what its number leaves out is the JVM's own start, which `process running for` adds.
